items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: CSR and financial performance — the evidence is mixed but tilts positive
items.claim: Friede, Busch and Bassen's 2015 meta-analysis aggregated over 2,000 studies on the link between ESG (environmental, social, governance) factors and corporate financial performance. What did it find?

options.text: ESG and financial performance are negatively related across the board
Around 90% of studies found a non-negative relationship; the majority showed positive correlation between ESG performance and financial performance, though magnitudes are modest
No study has examined this question
ESG is required to be at least cost-neutral by law

items.reveal:
Friede, Busch and Bassen (Journal of Sustainable Finance and Investment, 2015) reviewed 2,200 empirical studies dating back to the 1970s. About 90% reported non-negative ESG-CFP relationships; ~63% reported positive.

Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times Magazine essay ('The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits') argued the opposite. The empirical question turns out to be less stark than either side claims — the effect is usually positive but small, and depends on which ESG element and which industry.
items.why: Strategy debates about CSR are often conducted without reference to the evidence. The aggregate finding is messier than either 'CSR is profitable' or 'CSR is a cost' implies.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?
items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.
